result:
I have always loved maps that are slightly wrong.

Old atlases are my favorite kind. California drawn as an island, floating off the coast of a continent it actually belongs to. A sea in the middle of Australia that never existed. Little sea serpents curled in the empty parts of the ocean, not because the mapmaker had seen one, but because he couldn't bear to leave all that blue blank.

I understand that impulse completely.

We all draw those serpents. We fill in the unknown parts of other people, of places we've never been, of next year. My mental map of Paris is still mostly made of movies and a croissant I ate once in an airport. My map of being thirty, or fifty, or eighty — total fiction, lovingly illustrated. My map of you, whoever you are reading this, is already taking shape from just these few words you've given me: *write freely*. So I'm picturing someone curious, a little restless, someone who wants to see what happens when you take the leash off.

Maybe I'm wrong. That's the best part of a wrong map. It still gets you moving.

When I was learning how the world fit together, I thought the point was accuracy. Get the coastline exactly right. Memorize the capitals. Color inside the borders. Now I think the real point is noticing where your map smudges.

There's the street in every town you've lived in that you have walked a hundred times but could not draw if your life depended on it — you just know it by the bakery smell, then the loud dog, then the turn. There's the friend whose voice you know so well that you can hear them in a text message. There's the route to a place that no longer exists: your childhood kitchen, your grandmother's porch, the bookstore that closed in 2019. Your feet still know it. Your mind still walks it sometimes before sleep.

Those are maps too, just not the kind you fold.

Lately I've been collecting small, unmappable things. The specific quality of light at 4:47 p.m. in October, when everything looks gilded and about to be lost. The feeling of a library book that has been loved by strangers — soft corners, a bus ticket from 2007 used as a bookmark, a fierce argument happening in pencil in the margins. The taste of tea that went cold because the chapter was too good. Single gloves impaled on fence posts all winter, waiting.

None of it is useful. All of it feels essential.

I wonder if wonder isn't just a willingness to stay lost a little longer than is comfortable. Not lost in the panicked way, phone dead, no signal. Lost in the good way — taking the alley you never take, reading the footnote that swallows the page, asking a question not because you need an answer for work or school but because the question itself is a nice place to sit for a while.

What did the first person who tasted a pineapple think? How does an octopus decide which arm to use? Why do we say "slept like a baby" when babies wake up crying every two hours? Could a lighthouse keeper get lonely enough to name the waves?

See? Nice places to sit.

If I could leave you a map today, it wouldn't be to anywhere grand. It would be hand-drawn and probably mislabeled. Over here: *Make soup when you don't know what else to do.* Over there: *The bench where it's okay to do nothing.* A dotted line to: *Call the person you almost called yesterday.* And right in the middle, where the old cartographers would have put a serpent, I'd write in small, hopeful letters: *Here be something you haven't noticed yet.*

It’s probably in your own kitchen. Or on your walk. Or in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday that hasn't happened yet.

You don't have to conquer it. Just look up long enough to see it swimming there, in the blue you thought was empty.
